name: factory-kit
intent: Give one factory a table of named builder functions that the caller fills in, so it can create instances of types it never mentions by name - each product contributes its own construction rules instead of being hard-coded in a switch.
problem: A factory must produce objects from a set of implementation types that is not known when the factory is written - the set is configured by the caller, contributed by a plugin, or decided by a later module - so any if/switch over type names has to be edited, recompiled and retested every time a new type appears.
context: Applies where the set of constructible types is open at the edges of the program: game and editor content (items, entities, spells, level objects) registered by name, deserialization driven by a wire discriminator, plugin/integration hosts whose modules contribute implementations at startup, or any configuration-driven creation path. It pays off when construction differs per type (constructor arguments, injected dependencies, pre-computation) or when registration must stay outside the factory class; it assumes the key space is controlled by the registering side and that duplicate and unknown keys are handled deliberately.
benefits: Registration replaces modification: a new product type arrives as one register call from the module that owns it, and the factory itself never changes (open/closed principle).
Creation becomes one uniform, testable seam: 'give me a X' is a single call whose inputs (the registration table) can be built per test, in memory, without touching global state.
The caller owns the namespace: keys, aliases and precedence are configuration data rather than class names, so content designers or downstream packages can name things the factory has never heard of.
Construction detail hides behind the builder function: dependencies, pooling, pre-warming or validation can differ per product while callers depend only on the product abstraction.
Fits loader/plugin designs where the kit must be fully configured before the first create call, and gives one obvious place to audit which types are creatable.
tradeoffs: Compile-time safety is traded for runtime flexibility: a key typo or a missing registration fails at create time with an error instead of at compile time, and no IDE can follow key -> builder -> product.

The registry is shared mutable state with a lifetime: who may register, when registration closes, and whether a duplicate key overwrites or errors must be decided explicitly, and load order silently changes behaviour.
A second dispatch mechanism exists beside the type system, so readers must learn the table's conventions to find the concrete type behind a key.
Load-time self-registration (static initializers, link-time collection) adds failure modes the code does not show: undefined registration order and linkers dropping unreferenced units.
Every creation pays a table lookup plus a type-erased callable; negligible per object unless creation is in a hot loop.
The kit attracts unrelated creation policy (caching, scoping, validation) and drifts into a service locator, after which every dependency is a key lookup.

participants.responsibility: Holds the table from key to builder, exposes the registration step and the create(key) operation, and never names a concrete product type.
The name, enum value or type token a caller passes to create(); part of the public contract and the reason failures move from compile time to runtime.
Produces one concrete product; it is what registration installs, and it captures the dependencies and configuration that the registering module chose.
The abstraction the table is typed by and the only thing clients see; concrete products never appear in the kit.
Supplies the set of registrations - typically one configuration function or per-module init code - deciding which types this kit can build and with what dependencies.

use_cases: Game and engine content pipelines: item, weapon, entity or spell types registered by name so designers or mods add content without touching the factory. Godot's object system and Unreal's Actor Factories follow this pattern.

Polymorphic serialization and deserialization: kotlinx.serialization's SerializersModule, JSON-RPC discriminator fields, and Protocol Buffer Any types all use a Factory Kit registry to dispatch on a wire-format key to the correct builder.

Plugin and integration hosts: OSGi, Java ServiceLoader, Dart plugin_kit, and Gradle's plugin system each use runtime registration so modules contribute implementations at startup without the host enumerating them.
Test-data construction: tests register fakes or builders for the same keys the production path uses, so the kit becomes the seam that keeps construction swappable without touching the calling code.

Protocol and handler registries: an opcode or message name maps to the builder of the handler that processes it, so new message kinds arrive as registrations rather than as code changes in the dispatcher.

Dynamic UI and dashboard builders: a toolkit exposes widget types by name and receives registered builders from contributed modules, allowing a plugin to introduce entirely new widget kinds without updating the host framework.

Kubernetes API machinery: every API group adds its Go types to runtime.Scheme through AddToScheme/AddKnownTypeWithName, and the decoder then instantiates the Go struct registered for the incoming GroupVersionKind - a production Factory Kit whose duplicate registration panics at startup instead of failing later at decode time.

Terraform Plugin Framework: a provider's Resources() and DataSources() methods return slices of constructor functions, so Terraform dispatches the resource type name used in configuration to the constructor the provider registered - every provider fills its own kit without Terraform core enumerating resource types.

Godot ClassDB registration modes: modules call ClassDB::register_class<T>() (GDREGISTER_CLASS) in their register_types hook, and the GDREGISTER_ABSTRACT/INTERNAL/RUNTIME variants let each registering module decide per class whether creation by name is allowed at all - from scripts, from C++ only, or at runtime only.
avoid_when: The set of types is closed and known at compile time: a sealed hierarchy with exhaustive match (Kotlin, Scala, Swift, Rust enum, TypeScript discriminated union) or a plain switch is type-safe, shorter and compiler-checked.
One concrete implementation exists, or the choice is made once at startup: construct it directly, or use a single named constructor / factory method instead of a table.

A dependency-injection container already resolves by key or type (.NET keyed services, Spring beans, Java ServiceLoader discovery): register with the container instead of maintaining a second, competing registry.
Only behaviour varies, not construction: use Strategy or a dispatch table rather than a factory, so no product type is invented for the sake of a lookup key.
Products are already reachable by reflection and need no custom construction (class-name-to-instance is enough): a reflective instantiation call is simpler than a builder table.
anti_patterns: A registry that grows into a service locator: the kit starts caching instances and resuming unrelated services, so every dependency becomes a key lookup and the create call is the only thing anyone uses.
A global mutable table written from arbitrary call sites at arbitrary times, with no rule for duplicates, making behaviour depend on import or initialisation order.
Registering fully constructed instances instead of builders ('a registry of singletons'), which throws away the per-call construction the pattern exists for.
Feeding an external string (request parameter, file header, query value) straight into create(), letting the caller name any registered implementation, including privileged ones.
Replacing a type-safe closed hierarchy with a string-keyed registry purely to avoid a switch, losing compiler exhaustiveness for flexibility nobody needs.
design_principles: Open/closed principle: new products arrive through registration, not through edits to the factory.
Dependency inversion: the kit and its clients depend on the product abstraction and a builder signature, never on concrete types.
Single responsibility: who contributes types (registration) is separated from how instances are produced (builders) and from when they are made (create).
Inversion of control: the host is configured by its modules instead of enumerating them.
Information hiding: the table, its duplicate policy and its key resolution stay private to the kit.
best_practices: Keep registration explicit: use a configuration function, a module init list, or a build step instead of relying on undiscoverable load-order side effects such as static initializers.
Fail loudly on both duplicate and unknown keys, naming the offending key and the known ones; return null only if the product is genuinely optional.
Register builders — not constructed instances — and let each builder receive its dependencies as parameters from the registering module rather than capturing them from globals.
Narrow the key type wherever possible: prefer an enum, sealed set, or sealed class discriminator over free strings, and validate any key that originates from outside the program.
Close the table after the configuration phase — freeze, snapshot, or publish an immutable copy — and document exactly when registration is allowed.
Assert at startup (or in a test) that every key in the registry can actually be created; a broken builder would otherwise surface only at first use, far from the registration site.

Make the registry thread-safe when accessed from multiple threads: use a ConcurrentHashMap in Java/Kotlin, a concurrent Mutex in Swift, or atomic copy-on-write in functional languages. Freeze the table after registration is complete to eliminate data races.

Use separate registration functions per product type (a named builder per key) rather than a single generic register(key, fn) that accepts arbitrary strings, so typos surface as compile-time errors in languages that support it.

Distinguish between factory (create a new instance per call), lazy singleton (create once on first use), and eager singleton (create once at registration) — register the appropriate variant explicitly rather than mixing behaviours in one table.

In compiled languages, be aware that cross-module inlining can cause identical string keys to hash differently when keys are hashed by pointer address rather than content; use content-based hashing for keys that cross module boundaries.
sources: Chiusano, Paul and Bjarnason, Runar. Functional Programming in Scala (Manning, 2014), Chapter 2 'Singletons, Factories, and Builders' — the canonical origin of the Factory Kit pattern as a configurable object builder where the host defines the factory interface and callers register builder functions at startup.

Chiusano, Paul and Bjarnason, Runar. Scala Functional Programming Patterns (O'Reilly, 2014), Chapter 2 — extends the Factory Kit discussion with Scala-specific implementation idioms including the object-kit framing.

iluwatar. Java Design Patterns — Factory Kit (community catalog; 'Also known as: Object Kit, Toolkit'; 'Factory kit is a configurable object builder, a factory to create factories'), https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/factory-kit/

Kotlinlang. PolymorphicModuleBuilder and SerializersModule — kotlinx.serialization implements a Factory Kit–style registry for open polymorphism: a base type's known subclasses are registered at runtime, and the module dispatches on discriminator keys at decode time, https://kotlinlang.org/api/kotlinx.serialization/kotlinx-serialization-core/kotlinx.serialization.modules/-polymorphic-module-builder/

https://github.com/Kotlin/kotlinx.serialization/blob/master/docs/polymorphism.md — Kotlinx.serialization polymorphic registry guide demonstrating SerializersModule { polymorphic<Base> { subclass<Subclass>() } } as a real-world Factory Kit usage.

Diego Pacheco. 'Factory Kit Pattern' (2021) — the reverse-factory framing: the caller defines the creational rules within guardrails set by the host, https://diego-pacheco.blogspot.com/2021/10/factory-kit-pattern.html

hlongco/Factory on GitHub — a Swift dependency injection library using compile-time-safe Factory Kit registrations; the repository's issue tracker documents real thread-safety pitfalls (data races on lazy injection, cross-module key hashing regressions), https://github.com/hmlongco/Factory

https://github.com/hmlongco/Factory/issues/373 — Regression issue in Factory 3.1.0: in Release builds, StaticString keys hashed by pointer address instead of content, causing cross-module registration mismatches; a concrete illustration of the 'runtime key resolution' pitfall.

plugin_kit on pub.dev — a Dart plugin runtime implementing Factory Kit–style registry with priority-based resolution; FactoryWrapper, LazySingletonWrapper, and SingletonWrapper registrations demonstrate all three builder-lifecycle variants, https://pub.dev/packages/plugin_kit

Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides. Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) — Abstract Factory is 'also known as Kit'; Factory Kit preserves the family-creation concern but replaces factory-subclass-per-family with a runtime-registered table.
docs/design-patterns.md section 3, 'Extension, policy and compile-time variation' — 'Factory Kit | one factory dispatches over many registered types'.

Godot Engine documentation, 'Object class' — ClassDB is the engine's Factory Kit: classes register via ClassDB::register_class<T>() / GDREGISTER_CLASS and become instantiable by name from scripts, code or deserialization, with GDREGISTER_VIRTUAL/ABSTRACT/INTERNAL/RUNTIME variants deciding per class whether and where creation by name is allowed, https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/engine_details/architecture/object_class.html

Kubernetes apimachinery, pkg/runtime/scheme.go — runtime.Scheme registers Go types under a GroupVersionKind (AddKnownTypeWithName, reached via each group's AddToScheme), keeps the gvkToType map the decoder uses to construct the right object, and panics on conflicting registrations: a production Factory Kit with a loud duplicate-key policy, https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/v0.35.3/pkg/runtime/scheme.go

HashiCorp Terraform Plugin Framework, 'Providers' — provider.Resources() and DataSources() return slices of constructor functions that make each resource type creatable under the name practitioners write in configuration; the provider module fills the kit Terraform core dispatches against, https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/providers

Yuxin Wu, 'Registration Does Not Scale Well' (2023) — critique of global name->object registries: import-time registrations execute code early, storing instances instead of factories defeats lazy construction, and registered state does not survive multiprocessing workers; recommends lazy imports or name->module-path mappings over a global mutable kit, https://ppwwyyxx.com/blog/2023/Registration-Does-Not-Scale-Well/

cppstories, 'Factory with self-registering types' (2018) — trade-off analysis of self-registering versus centrally-declared factories in C++: open extensibility bought with hidden static-initialization order and linker-discarding failure modes, the same load-time pitfalls this pattern's best practices warn against, https://www.cppstories.com/2018/02/factory-selfregister/
